units.text: INT. ALL-NIGHT LAUNDROMAT - 3 A.M.
Forty dryers turn like slow, patient moons.
The windows have gone to black mirrors.
In the one plastic chair that isn't cracked, CATALINA SOTO-MERCADO, seventies, sits guarding a wicker basket on her lap as if it were a sleeping child.
Across the aisle, her grandson EZEKIEL, sixteen, all elbows and hood, stares at his phone and refuses to be in the building.
You said an hour, Abuela. It's been three.
units.name: EZEKIEL

units.text: Then sit. Fold something.
units.name: CATALINA

units.text: There's nothing to fold. It's all in the dryer. Mom's stuff. Dad's stuff.
units.name: EZEKIEL

units.text: Catalina's hand tightens on the basket.
A dryer thuds to a stop behind them.
Neither moves.
That is not your father's stuff.
units.name: CATALINA

units.text: Ezekiel pockets the phone and crosses the aisle in four strides.
He reaches for the basket.
She pulls it to her chest.
For a moment they hold opposite ends of it, nose to nose, a wicker tug-of-war under the buzzing light.
He left it. It's a shirt, it's a stupid shirt.
units.name: EZEKIEL

units.text: It is the shirt he was wearing the day he taught you to ride.
units.name: CATALINA

units.text: That I don't remember!
units.name: EZEKIEL

units.text: The basket tips.
A faded blue shirt slides out and lands between them, half open on the tile.
They both freeze, breath held, staring at it as if it might stand up.
Ezekiel kneels first.
Catalina follows, knees cracking, and together they lift it by the sleeves, like folding a flag with no ceremony.
Hold your end.
units.name: CATALINA
